advisor.summary: Reg. §1.469-2(f)(6) is a one-way street: net income from renting property to a business in which the taxpayer materially participates is recharacterized as non-passive, while a net loss on the same arrangement stays passive. The design is deliberately asymmetric — it stops owners from manufacturing passive income by paying themselves rent — and Krukowski settled its validity. The planning consequences are structural: self-rental income can never absorb passive losses from other investments, and accelerated deductions on a self-rented building (a cost segregation study, a heavy repair year) create a passive loss stranded next to non-passive business income unless the rental and the business are grouped as one activity under Reg. §1.469-4(d). Rent-setting within arm's-length bounds and the grouping decision have to precede the depreciation strategies, which is why this record is advisory: the value is sequencing and structure, not a computable deduction.
mechanics: The rule: rent property to a trade or business in which the taxpayer (or spouse) materially participates, and net rental income for the year is recharacterized non-passive under Reg. §1.469-2(f)(6) — while a net loss remains passive; the asymmetry never nets.

The standard fix is grouping the rental with the operating business as one activity under Reg. §1.469-4(d), available where ownership is proportionate or one activity is insubstantial — with the Rev. Proc. 2010-13 disclosure filed for the new grouping.

Rent level is a real lever within arm’s-length bounds: lower rent leaves income in the operating business, higher rent shifts it to the rental side where it is non-passive but escapes self-employment tax — comparables in the file keep the choice defensible.
A self-rental to a commonly controlled business generally remains a trade or business for the §199A deduction under Reg. §1.199A-1(b)(14), preserving QBI on the rental income.

Sequencing rule for the whole real-estate stack: the grouping decision comes before cost segregation or major repairs on a self-rented building, because an ungrouped building’s accelerated loss lands in the passive bucket beside non-passive business income.

authority.note: The self-rental recharacterization: income non-passive, losses still passive — the asymmetry the planning works around.
Upheld the regulation against a validity challenge — an attorney renting an office building to his own firm; the rule is settled law.
When a rental may be grouped with the operating business — proportionate ownership or insubstantiality — the principal structural fix.
Self-rented property leased to a commonly controlled business is treated as a trade or business for QBI purposes.
The written disclosure required when the grouping fix is elected.

requirements: A complete map of every arrangement where the client or spouse rents property to an entity they materially participate in.
A written, arm’s-length lease with rent supported by market comparables.
For the grouping fix: proportionate ownership (or insubstantiality) plus the Rev. Proc. 2010-13 disclosure.
A rent-level review before any year with major deductions planned on the building.
risks: The leading audit theory is treating self-rental income as passive to absorb other passive losses — the exact position Krukowski v. Commissioner, 279 F.3d 547 (7th Cir. 2002), forecloses; exam adjusts the character, the losses re-strand, and penalties follow.
Cost segregation on an ungrouped self-rented building is the classic sequencing error: an expensive study producing a stranded passive loss.
Rent far off market invites recharacterization of the arrangement itself and collateral payroll and state scrutiny.
The grouping is binding and reshapes loss release at disposition — model the exit before filing the disclosure.
Retirement or role changes end material participation and flip the analysis; the structure needs review at every ownership or participation change.
stateNotes: Conformity: the recharacterization is a federal character rule that states inherit through their federal starting points — state passive-loss treatment follows the federal result in conforming states.
Missouri conforms via federal AGI (RSMo §143.121); no Missouri-specific filing attaches to the grouping or the lease.
PTET interaction: rent paid by an electing operating entity is a deduction against its PTET base while the rental income sits outside it — re-run the PTET projection whenever the rent level is reset.
reviewChecklist: Self-rental arrangements inventoried, with material participation confirmed on the operating side.
Lease written, current, and rent tied to retained comparables.
Grouping analysis completed and the disclosure filed where elected — before depreciation strategies launch.
QBI treatment of the rental confirmed under the common-control rule.
Exit and disposition consequences of any grouping modeled and documented.

client.teaser: Own the building your business rents? A one-way tax rule needs planning before it costs you.
client.headline: Renting to your own business: get ahead of the one-way rule
plainEnglish: Many owners hold their building personally and rent it to their company. Smart for liability. But a special tax rule applies: if the building makes money, that profit counts as active income. If it loses money, the loss is passive — and often stuck.

This one-way rule surprises people twice. Rent income from your own company cannot soak up losses from other investments. And big spending on the building — renovations, fast depreciation — can create a loss that sits in a bucket where it does nothing.

The fixes are structural and simple. Often one election treats the building and the business as a single activity. Rent gets set at a documented market rate. Done before the big deductions, the rule stops working against you.
client.analogy: It is like a one-way valve in your plumbing — we cannot remove it, but we can route the pipes so it never blocks your flow.
benefits: Keeps large building deductions usable instead of stranded
Rent set where it saves the most across the business and the building
Heads off a common and costly audit surprise
steps: WE review the lease, the ownership, and the rent level.
WE set the structure and elections so future deductions land where they count.
WE document the market rent so the setup stands scrutiny.
YOU sign the updated lease and keep payments flowing per its terms.
clientCommitments: Pay rent exactly as the lease states, through the business account
Tell us before major building spending or any ownership change

annualMaintenance: Annual rent-level review against current comparables
Re-check material participation and ownership alignment each year
Sequence any planned building deductions through the structure first
deliverables: Self-rental structure memo with rent-setting analysis
Grouping election and disclosure filings where chosen
